cells.tense: The pen is in your hand right now, and you get to choose which way this goes.
cells.ask: Commit to one direction this week — pick a single thing and put it in front of someone. The timing is the practice.
cells.core:
You carry a fire that shows. It's not performance — the excitement is real and it travels, which is why people move toward what you're doing. Asking, exploring, starting things: that's the operating mode, and you're in it on purpose.

Holding it steady has a cost. A spark can read as a promise you haven't decided to make yet, and the people pulled in by it need to know which way you're actually facing. That's where the figuring comes in — not to cool the fire down, but to give it a line to travel along. You don't need the whole route. You need the next real choice and the honesty to say it out loud, so the heat lands somewhere and doesn't just glow.
cells.sheetLine: The fire is real — give it a direction you'll stand behind.
cells.verb: lighting the fire and taking the first step before the whole route is known

cells.tense: You are living three steps ahead, in a version of this that has not happened yet.
cells.ask: Stop one fire from being lit this week. Sit with the not-knowing and listen before the next step.
cells.core:
The fire has gotten ahead of you. You're already in the room where it worked, already answering questions nobody's asked, already carrying people along to a place you haven't reached. The excitement started as wanting to find out — somewhere along the way it turned into needing to be certain, out loud, ahead of time.

What's happening is that direction gets decided before the information arrives. The rush to shine skips the listening that would actually tell you which way to steer. That's why you're tired in a way the work alone doesn't explain: some of the energy is going into staying ahead of a future that keeps not arriving. Dimming nothing is the point. Let the next thing be unknown for a while, and find out you're fine in that room.

cells.tense: There was a moment when you set the fire down, and you have not picked it back up.
cells.ask: Tend one small thing today — water a plant, cook something real, put one direction in motion with your hands.
cells.core:
The ability to choose a direction and say 'this, not that' is there. What stopped is the showing of it — the exploring, the asking, the visible aliveness of wanting something. It hasn't come back out, though the pull toward it is still in you.

So the work now isn't to force the fire back on. That just comes out strained. It's to get your hands on something small and let caring for it do the lighting. Structure at this scale — a thing you tend, a direction you move through by doing — is what gives energy back to the part of you that picks and commits. Start with what's in front of you, and let the next choice follow from there.
cells.sheetLine: The ability to choose is still there — the showing of it went quiet.
cells.verb: lighting the fire and taking the first step before the whole route is known
cells.place: the point where a direction gets chosen and held to

cells.tense: You are already setting the direction here, and you are describing it as circumstances.
cells.ask: Name a result you've been treating as inevitable and say out loud that you chose it. Then stand behind it.
cells.core:
You're directing things. People are following a line you drew — the way you showed up, the thing you kept starting, the mood you set — and it's landing. But when you talk about it, it comes out as though the situation decided itself and you were just there. The steering is happening. Your ownership of it isn't.

The fire is genuine. What's missing is the saying-so, the plain acknowledgment that this direction is yours and you're the one holding it. That's a weight, which is probably why it's been left with circumstance instead. The steadier form of this is strength that holds a line without gripping it — the kind you get from owning the choice and letting it stand. That's the part still looking for a home.
cells.sheetLine: You're steering. You're just calling it circumstance.
